gloss: strive with and prevail; rule, be prince; prince, chief
summary: שָׂרָה is to strive with someone and hold out until one prevails: Jacob שָׂרִיתָ “strove with God and with men and prevailed”, and so was named יִשְׂרָאֵל (Gen 32:29). Hosea retells the night with שָׂרָה and then וַיָּשַׂר, the form that elsewhere means “he ruled” (Hos 12:4–5; Jdg 9:22), and the root’s other words are about rule: מִשְׂרָה “dominion” on the shoulder of the child who is שַׂר שָׁלוֹם (Isa 9:5–6), the verb שָׂרַר “rule, act as prince”, the שַׂר who is a king’s official, a commander or the chief of a people, and in Daniel an angel set over a nation, and שָׂרָה “princess”. Arabic šariya “persist, persevere; persist in contention” answers the striving, and Akkadian šarru “king” the ruling.

words.summary: One who holds rule under or beside a king, or over a group: the king’s officials, the chief over a body of men or a work, the commander of an army or of a thousand, the heads of a people or city, and in Joshua and Daniel the angels who lead Yahweh’s host and stand over nations. Set beside מֶלֶךְ “king” and שֹׁפֵט “judge” again and again. About 420 uses.

senses.definition: One of the great men about a king, who serve him and share his rule; named beside the king as the governing class of a land.

evidence.note: שָׂרֵי פַרְעֹה saw her and praised her to Pharaoh: the men of his court.
“Give me a king and שָׂרִים”: the two make up the government Israel asked for.
Many days without king and without שַׂר.
A feast for all his שָׂרִים and servants … and the שָׂרֵי הַמְּדִינוֹת before him.
All the שָׂרִים sitting in the scribe’s chamber of the king’s house.
Woe to the land whose king is a boy and whose שָׂרִים feast in the morning; blessed the land whose שָׂרִים eat in due season.
They make the king glad with their wickedness, and שָׂרִים with their lies.
The שָׂרֵי יְהוּדָה came and bowed to the king, and he listened to them.
All the שָׂרֵי מֶלֶךְ בָּבֶל sat in the middle gate.

senses.gloss: chief, overseer of a body or a work
senses.definition: The one set over a particular group, office or task: the chief of the guard, of the cupbearers, of the herds, of the forced labour, of the city, of the priests.

evidence.note: וְשַׂמְתָּם שָׂרֵי מִקְנֶה עַל־אֲשֶׁר לִי: “set them as chiefs of livestock over what is mine”.
שַׂר הַמַּשְׁקִים and שַׂר הָאוֹפִים, the chief of the cupbearers and the chief of the bakers.
Potiphar, שַׂר הַטַּבָּחִים, chief of the guard (also Gen 39:1).
שָׂרֵי מִסִּים set over Israel to afflict them with their burdens.
Zebul שַׂר הָעִיר, the city’s governor (also 1Ki 22:26; 2Ki 23:8).
שַׂר הַסָּרִיסִים gave them names.
Weighed before שָׂרֵי הַכֹּהֲנִים וְהַלְוִיִּם וְשָׂרֵי הָאָבוֹת.
שַׂר חֲצִי פֶּלֶךְ יְרוּשָׁלִָם, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem (and through Neh 3:19).

senses.definition: The leader of an army, or of a unit of a thousand, a hundred, fifty or ten.

evidence.note: Able men, fearing God, men of truth, hating gain: set them שָׂרֵי אֲלָפִים שָׂרֵי מֵאוֹת שָׂרֵי חֲמִשִּׁים וְשָׂרֵי עֲשָׂרֹת.
Phicol שַׂר־צְבָאוֹ, the commander of Abimelech’s army.
Abner, שַׂר צְבָאוֹ of Saul.
Naaman, שַׂר־צְבָא מֶלֶךְ־אֲרָם.
The officers of the army, שָׂרֵי הָאֲלָפִים וְשָׂרֵי הַמֵּאוֹת, coming from the war.
The king will appoint for himself שָׂרֵי אֲלָפִים וְשָׂרֵי חֲמִשִּׁים.
A שַׂר חֲמִשִּׁים and his fifty.
The horse smells the battle afar off, רַעַם שָׂרִים, the thunder of the captains.

senses.definition: One of the heads of a people, tribe or town, who lead and decide for it; or one who rules over a people as such.

evidence.note: מִי שָׂמְךָ לְאִישׁ שַׂר וְשֹׁפֵט עָלֵינוּ: “who set you as a שַׂר and judge over us?” Quoted in Acts 7:27, 35, where God sends that same Moses as ruler and redeemer.
The well which שָׂרִים dug, which נְדִיבֵי הָעָם, the nobles of the people, delved.
He wrote down שָׂרֵי סֻכּוֹת and her elders, seventy-seven men.
The people, שָׂרֵי גִלְעָד, ask who will be head over all Gilead.
שָׂרֵי מוֹאָב, Balak’s envoys.
שָׂרֵי יְהוּדָה … שָׂרֵי זְבֻלוּן שָׂרֵי נַפְתָּלִי, the leaders of the tribes in procession.
“Instead of your fathers shall be your sons; you will make them שָׂרִים in all the earth.”
A king will reign in righteousness, וּלְשָׂרִים לְמִשְׁפָּט יָשֹׂרוּ.
Exo 2:14 quoted: “Who made you ἄρχοντα καὶ δικαστὴν over us?”
“This one God sent as ἄρχοντα καὶ λυτρωτήν”.

senses.definition: Among the names of the child born to bear the dominion: the prince whose rule is peace, on David’s throne.

evidence.note: וַתְּהִי הַמִּשְׂרָה עַל־שִׁכְמוֹ … שַׂר שָׁלוֹם: the שַׂר who bears the מִשְׂרָה.
Of the increase of the dominion and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David.

senses.gloss: angelic prince, leader of a host
senses.definition: An angel who leads Yahweh’s host, or stands over a nation: Michael is Israel’s שַׂר; Persia and Greece have each a שַׂר who stands against him.

evidence.note: אֲנִי שַׂר־צְבָא־יַהְוֶה, the one with the drawn sword before Jericho; Joshua bows, and is told the place is holy (5:15).
שַׂר מַלְכוּת פָּרַס stood against me twenty-one days, and Michael, אַחַד הַשָּׂרִים הָרִאשֹׁנִים, came to help me.
To fight with שַׂר פָּרָס, and then שַׂר יָוָן comes.
None holds with me in these but מִיכָאֵל שַׂרְכֶם, “Michael your prince”.
Michael הַשַּׂר הַגָּדוֹל הָעֹמֵד עַל־בְּנֵי עַמֶּךָ, at the time of trouble when the people is delivered.
The horn magnified itself even to שַׂר הַצָּבָא, and the continual was taken from him.
He will stand against שַׂר־שָׂרִים, and be broken without hand.

This Moses God sent ἄρχοντα καὶ λυτρωτήν.
Jesus Christ, ὁ ἄρχων τῶν βασιλέων τῆς γῆς.

parallels.note: King and שָׂרִים together are the rulers of a land.
Prince and judge: those who rule and decide.
Princes and elders of a town or of Pharaoh’s house.

opposites.note: The world upside down: servants on horses and שָׂרִים walking like servants; a servant ruling over שָׂרִים.

phrases.gloss: commanders of thousands and of hundreds
your princes are rebels (a play on the sounds)

words.summary: The feminine of שַׂר: a lady of a royal or noble house. Five uses; the same spelling is Sarah’s name (Gen 17:15), which has its own entry.

senses.definition: A woman of a ruling house or of the nobility, set beside kings and opposite concubines and forced labourers.

evidence.note: נָשִׁים שָׂרוֹת seven hundred, and three hundred concubines: wives of rank against concubines.
Kings your foster-fathers, וְשָׂרוֹתֵיהֶם your nursing mothers.
שָׂרָתִי בַּמְּדִינוֹת הָיְתָה לָמַס: the princess among the provinces has become a forced labourer.
The wise ones of Sisera’s mother’s שָׂרוֹת answer her.
שָׂרוֹת פָּרַס וּמָדַי will speak so to all the king’s שָׂרִים.

opposites.note: The princess become a forced labourer.

words.summary: To act as שַׂר: to rule over a people or a house. Hosea uses its qal וַיָּשַׂר of Jacob’s struggle in parallel with שָׂרָה, so the two verbs meet in “prevail”.

senses.definition: To exercise rule over a people, a land or a household.

evidence.note: וַיָּשַׂר אֲבִימֶלֶךְ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵל שָׁלֹשׁ שָׁנִים.
A king יִמְלָךְ in righteousness and princes יָשֹׂרוּ in justice: “reign” and “rule” in parallel.
בִּי שָׂרִים יָשֹׂרוּ, by wisdom princes rule, and nobles, all judges of righteousness.
That every man should be שֹׂרֵר בְּבֵיתוֹ, ruling in his house.

senses.definition: In Hosea’s retelling of Jacob at Peniel, to contend with and prevail over the angel, in the place of שָׂרָה in the line before.

evidence.note: וַיָּשַׂר אֶל־מַלְאָךְ וַיֻּכָל, “he strove (or prevailed) with the angel and overcame”, after שָׂרָה אֶת־אֱלֹהִים in 12:4.

stems.gloss: make oneself a prince, lord it over

senses.definition: To take rule to oneself over others; Korah’s company’s charge against Moses.

evidence.note: כִּי־תִשְׂתָּרֵר עָלֵינוּ גַּם־הִשְׂתָּרֵר, “that you make yourself a prince over us, even make yourself a prince!”

senses.definition: To set up rulers; in parallel with הִמְלִיךְ “make kings”.

evidence.note: הֵם הִמְלִיכוּ וְלֹא מִמֶּנִּי הֵשִׂירוּ וְלֹא יָדָעְתִּי: they made kings, but not from me; they made princes, and I did not know.

evidence.locator: Jdg.9.22, וַיָּשַׂר → ἦρχεν; Isa.32.1, יָשֹׂרוּ → ἄρχουσιν

evidence.note: Those who seem to rule (ἄρχειν) the Gentiles lord it over them; “it shall not be so among you”.
The root of Jesse, who rises ἄρχειν ἐθνῶν, to rule the Gentiles.

parallels.note: Reign and rule: the king reigns, princes rule; they made kings, they made princes.
Hosea’s two verbs for Jacob’s struggle.

words.gloss: strive with, persist against and prevail
words.summary: Two uses, both of Jacob’s night at Peniel, where they explain the name יִשְׂרָאֵל. Gen 32 shows what the striving was: a wrestling (וַיֵּאָבֵק) until dawn, Jacob holding on until he was blessed.

senses.definition: To contend with someone and hold on, not letting go, so as to prevail; said of Jacob with God (in the angel) and with men.

evidence.note: כִּי־שָׂרִיתָ עִם־אֱלֹהִים וְעִם־אֲנָשִׁים וַתּוּכָל: “for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed”; the reason for the name יִשְׂרָאֵל.
In the womb he took his brother by the heel (עָקַב), וּבְאוֹנוֹ שָׂרָה אֶת־אֱלֹהִים, and in his strength he strove with God.
A man wrestled (וַיֵּאָבֵק) with him until dawn; touched in the thigh, Jacob says “I will not let you go unless you bless me”: the striving is holding on.
He prevailed (וַיֻּכָל); he wept and sought his favour: how the striving won.

evidence.locator: Gen.32.29, שָׂרִיתָ → ἐνίσχυσας; Hos.12.4, שָׂרָה → ἐνίσχυσεν; Hos.12.5, וַיָּשַׂר → ἐνίσχυσεν

evidence.note: An angel from heaven appeared to him, ἐνισχύων αὐτόν, strengthening him, and being in an agony he prayed the more earnestly.
Saul took food ἐνίσχυσεν, and was strengthened.

parallels.note: The wrestling that Gen 32:29 calls striving.

opposites.note: Hosea sets the two names side by side: in the womb he took the heel (עָקַב, Jacob), in his strength he strove with God (שָׂרָה, Israel). Esau had read the first name as “supplant” (Gen 27:36).

words.summary: Two uses, both Isa 9, of the rule laid on the shoulder of the child born to David’s throne. Its sense is rule, the sense of שַׂר and שָׂרַר, though it is spelled from שׂרה.

senses.definition: The rule or government of a kingdom, borne by its ruler and increasing without end.

evidence.note: וַתְּהִי הַמִּשְׂרָה עַל־שִׁכְמוֹ: the rule is on his shoulder, and his name is שַׂר שָׁלוֹם.
לְמַרְבֵּה הַמִּשְׂרָה וּלְשָׁלוֹם אֵין קֵץ עַל־כִּסֵּא דָוִד וְעַל־מַמְלַכְתּוֹ: dominion set with David’s throne and his kingdom.
Gabriel: God will give him the throne of his father David, he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end; Isa 9:6’s “no end” expounded.

parallels.note: The dominion is David’s throne and kingdom.

words.summary: Formed from the name יִשְׂרָאֵל with the ending ־ִי of belonging: one of Israel’s people. Five uses. Its tie to the root is through the name (see names/yisrael), not a meaning of its own, so no cognate is named on it.

senses.definition: Of Israel’s people, as against a foreigner.

evidence.note: The son of an יִשְׂרְאֵלִית woman and an Egyptian man fought with הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי, the Israelite man.
The son of the יִשְׂרְאֵלִית blasphemed the Name.
Ithra הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי, called “Jether the Ishmaelite” in 1Ch 2:17.

cognates.gloss: persist, persevere; (III) persist in contention, wrangle with; (X) strive, exert oneself
cognates.note: Lane’s sources give šariya of a man “persisted, or persevered, in an affair”, of a horse “persisted in his pace”, and of anger; form III yušārīhi “he persists in contention, litigation, or wrangling, with him”; form X “he strove, or exerted himself … in his religion”. This is the striving of Gen 32:29: contending and holding on. Arabic š (ش) answers Hebrew שׂ, and the final y the final ה. One authority in Lane derives form III from a doubled root, “originally يُشَارِرُ”, the same pairing of a final-weak with a doubled root as Hebrew שׂרה beside שׂרר. Lane’s other šarā, “sell, buy”, is a separate meaning and has no bearing here.

p. 1545, شَارَاهُ 3 (n22260): “he persists in contention, litigation, or wrangling, with him”
p. 1545, استشرى 10 (n22264): “he strove, or exerted himself … in his religion”

cognates.note: Akkadian’s commonest word for king, with its feminine and abstract: the same consonants as שַׂר, שָׂרָה “princess” and מִשְׂרָה “dominion”. Akkadian š covers Hebrew שׂ as well as שׁ. In Hebrew the word has come down a rank, from the king to the men who rule under or beside him; it keeps “rule”.
Recorded in Wiktionary’s Phoenician only; Krahmalkov’s Phoenician-Punic Dictionary has no such entry under Š-R, so the attestation is unchecked.

Jewish Aramaic of the Talmud and Midrash (“the chief of the sea”, Y. Snh. VII), the same as Hebrew שַׂר. It may be the Hebrew word taken into the rabbis’ Aramaic rather than an Aramaic word of its own; Biblical Aramaic and the Peshitta have no word of the root.

evidence.note: Y. Snh. VII, 25ᵈ; Lev. R. s. 5.

doctrine.statement: Jacob was left alone and a man wrestled with him until dawn; when the man touched his thigh and put it out of joint, Jacob would not let him go unless he blessed him, and he was named Israel “for you have striven with God and with men and prevailed” (Gen 32:25–29). Hosea tells what the striving was: “he prevailed; he wept and sought his favour” (Hos 12:5), and he calls the people to the same: “turn to your God, keep mercy and judgment, and wait on your God continually” (Hos 12:7). Paul asks the Romans to “strive together with me in prayers to God for me” (Rom 15:30), and Epaphras is “always striving for you in prayers” (Col 4:12). From the verses: Jacob did not overcome by strength, for a touch disabled him; he prevailed by holding on and pleading for the blessing, and that persistent pleading is the striving that scripture commends.

Genesis says Jacob strove “with God” (עִם־אֱלֹהִים) and named the place Peniel, “for I have seen God face to face” (Gen 32:29, 31); Hosea says he strove with God and then “strove with the angel (מַלְאָךְ) and prevailed” (Hos 12:4–5). Jacob himself puts the two together when he blesses Joseph’s sons: “the God who shepherded me … the angel who redeemed me from all evil” (Gen 48:15–16). Yahweh says of the angel he sends before Israel, “my name is in him” (Exo 23:20–21), and John writes that no one has seen God at any time (Jhn 1:18). From the verses: the one Jacob wrestled was an angel bearing God’s name, and to meet him face to face was to meet God in his messenger.

Esau said of his brother, “is he not rightly named Jacob? for he has supplanted me these two times”, and Isaac said he came “with deceit” (Gen 27:35–36). The name Israel was given to the same man for prevailing with God (Gen 32:29) and confirmed at Bethel (Gen 35:10), and his sons became בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, the people Yahweh speaks to in his feasts and leads through the wilderness (Lev 23:2; Num 10:29). Isaiah foresees men who will say “I am Yahweh’s” and surname themselves by the name of Israel (Isa 44:5). Jesus calls Nathanael “truly an Israelite, in whom is no deceit” (Jhn 1:47); Paul writes that “not all who are of Israel are Israel”, but the children of the promise are counted as the seed (Rom 9:6–8), that those who are Christ’s are Abraham’s seed and heirs by promise (Gal 3:29), and he blesses “the Israel of God” (Gal 6:16). From the verses: the name describes what God made of the supplanter, and it belongs in full to those who share that change and the promise, not to descent alone.

Isaiah says “a child is born to us, a son is given to us, and the dominion (הַמִּשְׂרָה) is on his shoulder”, names him among other names שַׂר שָׁלוֹם, and says that of the increase of the dominion and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, “from now and for ever” (Isa 9:5–6). Gabriel tells Mary that the son she will conceive and bear will be given the throne of his father David, will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luk 1:31–33). From the verses: the one who bears the dominion is a son born of David’s house, and his rule is exercised on David’s throne over a kingdom that will not end.

Psalm 45, whose words to the king Hebrews applies to the Son (Heb 1:8–9), tells him “instead of your fathers shall be your sons; you will make them שָׂרִים in all the earth” (Psa 45:17). Isaiah sees a king reign in righteousness and princes rule (יָשֹׂרוּ) in justice (Isa 32:1). Jesus tells the twelve that they will sit on twelve thrones judging the tribes of Israel (Mat 19:28), and the redeemed sing that they have been made kings and priests “and we shall reign on the earth” (Rev 5:10). Jesus also says that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, but “whoever would be great among you shall be your servant” (Mrk 10:42–43), and Moses was told to choose as שָׂרִים men who fear God, men of truth, hating gain (Exo 18:21). From the verses: the king’s rule will be shared with those he makes princes, on the earth, and the princes fit for it are those who serve and fear God.

Before Jericho Joshua met one with a drawn sword who said, “I am שַׂר־צְבָא־יַהְוֶה”, and Joshua bowed and was told to put off his shoes, for the place was holy (Jos 5:13–15). Daniel is told of a שַׂר of Persia who withstood the angel speaking to him, and a שַׂר of Greece to come, and of Michael, “one of the chief princes”, “your prince”, who alone holds with him (Dan 10:13, 20–21). “At that time Michael shall stand up, the great prince who stands over the sons of your people”, and there will be a time of trouble, the people will be delivered, and many who sleep in the dust will awake (Dan 12:1–2). The horn of Dan 8 magnifies itself against the שַׂר of the host and stands against the שַׂר שָׂרִים, and is broken “without hand” (Dan 8:11, 25), as the stone cut out without hands breaks the image (Dan 2:34, 45). From the verses: Yahweh’s host has a prince, Michael is set over Daniel’s people for their deliverance and the resurrection at the end, and the power that sets itself against the Prince of princes falls by no human hand.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13. Root key: the task named ישׂראל, but the corpus files Israel (u.ce.ab) under שׂרה, so this is the root entry for שׂרה, and Israel has its own name entry (names/yisrael.json); xj.ak.ah is the Biblical Aramaic Israel (Ezra), root key ישׂראל, also on the name entry. Included as a by-form, root key שׂרר: שַׂר (u.cm.ab), שָׂרָה “princess” (u.cm.ad) and the verb שָׂרַר (u.cm.ac). The reason is scripture’s own: Hosea puts שָׂרָה (12:4) and וַיָּשַׂר (12:5) side by side for the one event, and the same וַיָּשַׂר means “ruled” in Jdg 9:22; and מִשְׂרָה, spelled from שׂרה, means “rule”. If the reviewer prefers a separate שׂרר entry, the three words move with their bdb keys. Counts: u.ce.aa has 31 tokens, of which 29 are the name Sarah (u.cm.ae) by spelling; the verb proper has only Gen 32:29 and Hos 12:4. u.cm.ab includes Sarai’s 12 tokens by spelling. MACULA analyses Hos 12:5 וַיָּשַׂר and Hos 8:4 הֵשִׂירוּ under שׂוּר, and 1Ch 20:3 וַיָּשַׂר “sawed” is שׂוּר “saw”, left out. Left out as names (own entries, not written here): שָׂרָה Sarah (u.cm.ae), שָׂרַי Sarai (u.cm.af), שְׂרָיָה(וּ) Seraiah (u.ce.ad), שֶׂרַח Serah (u.cf.ac; its link to the root is not clear), שַׁוְשָׁא Shavsha (v.cc.af, a variant of Seraiah in 1Ch 18:16). Cross-references with no tokens: j.dr.ab, m.dr.aw, u.cg.ae, u.ca.ab, u.cd.ad, u.cg.ad. Open questions: (1) Whether strive and rule are one older root or two that met; Arabic šariya “persist, contend” fits the striving, Akkadian šarru the rule, and no one language shows both. (2) Doctrine “michael-the-great-prince” leaves the שַׂר of Persia and of Greece as the text has them; check the reviewer’s reading. (3) Doctrine “prince-of-peace” does not discuss the other names of Isa 9:5. Leads not followed: Ugaritic (no śr “prince” found in Segert or Fisher); Ge’ez śārara “found, establish” (Anderson–Moser SEM000911) not checked in Dillmann and not recorded, since its meaning differs; Phoenician šr only in Wiktionary; Old South Arabic not checked; Wiktionary’s Arabic سرر “gladden” is not a regular match (س, not ش) and is not recorded.
